Orthocenter and Three Equal Circles

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: the three circles through two corners and the point where a triangle's heights meet are the same size as the circle around the whole triangle.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names, heights, the equal diameters or the outside triangle.
Look for the math

Start with any triangle. Each pair of corners and the point where the three heights meet determines a circle. The surprise is that all three of those circles are the same size as the circumcircle of the triangle you started with. Drag a corner and see if you can break that.

The point where the heights meet

The three lines from a corner straight across the opposite side meet at the orthocenter H. For ABC, the circle through B, C and H has the same radius as the circle through A, B and C. The same goes for the circles through C,A,H and A,B,H. "Equal" here means equal in size, not the very same circle: the three new circles pass through different points.

Reflecting the point across a side

Here is the page's first proof. Let the altitude from A meet BC at Ha, and let it cross the circumcircle again at P. Reflecting H in BC lands exactly on P, so Ha is the midpoint of H P. Triangles HBC and PBC then have the same base and the same height, hence they are congruent and their circumcircles are equal. But P is already on the circumcircle of ABC, so that circle is the circle through B, C and H.

Three equal diameters

Write the corners as vectors from the circumcenter O. Then H = A + B + C − 2O. The point opposite H on the circle through B,C,H is A′ = B + C − A, and cyclically B′ = C + A − B and C′ = A + B − C. So A, B and C are the midpoints of B′C′, C′A′ and A′B′: A′B′C′ is the anticomplementary triangle of ABC, with four times its area and H as its circumcenter. The three diameters HA′, HB′ and HC′ all equal 2R, the circumdiameter. Tick "Show hint" and "Show premise" to see the right angles which say that those segments really are diameters.

What was checked

The logic test checks all of the page's claims on the opening shape, ten hand-picked triangles, a grid of 400 shapes and 700 random ones: equal radii, equal diameters, H as the outer triangle's circumcenter, the three straight lines A′BC′ and so on, the four congruent triangles, the area ratio four, and the reflected point on the circumcircle. Every number is compared with a second transcription of the applet's own bytecode and with the closed formulas above; all of them agree. A triangle that is flat, or right-angled so one of the three circles degenerates, is refused, as the applet's own guard did. The live cut-the-knot page now has a GeoGebra figure instead of the Java applet; a 2010 capture shows the original EqualCirclesOrthocenter applet on that address. That old page also passed a ShowNames parameter the applet never read, so all four boxes start unchecked here, and the "New diagram" button is an addition for exploration.

Tick "Show premise" and then "Show hint": the six little square corners at A, B and C show why the lines from H are diameters of equal circles.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
